newsitem.title: JAPAN: INSTANT VIEW-Japan Jan current account surplus.
newsitem.headline: INSTANT VIEW-Japan Jan current account surplus.

text.p: The following is a selection of analysts' reactions to Japan's current account data for January released on Thursday, which showed a surplus of 150.7 billion yen compared with a surplus of 32.6 billion yen a year earlier.

"There are two reasons the surplus is going up. One, because the yen has been so weak for the past year and a half and the other is that domestic demand is going to be very dull. (U.S. Deputy Treasury Secretary) Summers knows the surplus is going up and was presumably trying to get a commitment from Japan to stimulate its economy, but apparently didn't succeed."
"It's a disappointment (in that a deficit had been predicted)."

"The year-on-year comparison in the month of January does not mean anything much...A weak yen has been shifting trade fundamentals and if the yen stays at the current level, the trade surplus is going to increase. The Finance Ministry earlier this week announced that Japan's customs-cleared trade surplus rose 53.3 percent."

"High crude oil prices and a weak yen had been pushing up import values, therefore dampening surplus figures. But when those price factors are gone, we could fear a sharp increase in the surplus that could possibly cause some worries in the U.S.-Japan trade issues."
"We are actually looking for the first positive increase in Japan's trade surplus in February since November 1994."
"January is enormously volatile. There were fewer working days in that month."

Asked if the rise in Japan's current account surplus in January could be a major point of contention between Japan and the United States, Berryman said: "I think this has basically passed its sell-by date as a sexy market issue. The U.S. is now on the verge of taking trade problems with China more seriously... I don't think these figures either potentially or in terms of markets are all that sexy any more."
